To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) hematopoietic cell populations can be identified which have distinct in vivo repopulation properties; and (ii) the repopulation properties of these cells can be maintained in vivo but can change dramatically in culture.
hematopoietic progenitor cells can be isolated from adult bone marrow that are highly enriched for the ability to reconstitute the hematopoietic system of a recipient.

the hematopoietic repopulation patterns obtained from single cell transplants of adult mouse marrow cells can be stable in vivo for up to 6 months and can also change rapidly in vitro, suggesting that the in vivo environment is critical to maintain the original repopulation pattern of the transplanted cell.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular mechanisms that regulate stem cells.
the mechanisms by which hematopoietic progenitors are regulated in the bone marrow microenvironment and how these mechanisms may be perturbed in hematologic diseases.
the mechanisms underlying hematopoietic cell differentiation, and in particular the regulation of the balance of hematopoietics cells in the bone marrow.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are two or more types of stem cells in the bone marrow of adult mice, each with a different pattern of differentiation in vivo.
the in vivo repopulation patterns of the original cells were maintained in the majority of the clones, but the in vitro repopulation patterns were not maintained.
there is a spectrum of hematopoietically competent cells in bone marrow, and that these cells have a variety of differentiation potentials.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are multiple types of stem cells that can repopulate the hematopoietic system in a long term manner.

hematopoietic repopulation is not a unitary process, and that the hematopoietic system can support distinct repopulation programs in parallel, each of which may be associated with distinct biological properties.
the long term repopulating ability of primitive hematopoietc cells can be maintained in a stable manner in vivo, but the ability to maintain a distinct differentiation program is more labile.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the in vivo repopulation potential of a hematopoietic cell can change rapidly in vitro.

the differentiation program of a primitive hematopoietetic cell, which is a stem cell, can change rapidly in vitro, and that this is a property that we can exploit to generate cells of interest for therapeutic purposes.
the in vivo repopulation behavior of a single hematopoietic cell is not fixed but rather depends on the in vitro conditions under which it is maintained.
